title: Negative result is uninformative: no positive control, recipe never shown able to gain
quote: means we have no positive reference: the nulls above
explanation:
The paper concedes that no arm improves, including train-on-gold, and attributes this to the recipe (LoRA r=16 on q/v only, 1 epoch, fresh adapter from base each round, fp16, loss over the prompt, 512 limit). But then the experiment cannot discriminate between 'self-training does not help a 1.5B model', 'this recipe cannot move a 1.5B model in the right direction' and 'the pipeline has a bug'; the MDE calculation says what could be seen only if an effect existed, not that this apparatus can produce one. Cheap positive controls were available and not run: distilling from a stronger teacher whose correct solutions the authors already have (the 7B solutions), training on solutions for the exam problems (memorisation check), a larger/different recipe with tuned LR, or injecting a synthetic effect of known size. The train-on-gold arm is not a positive control because it changes style and length and degrades accuracy. Without a demonstration of sensitivity, the title/abstract claim that reads as an answer to 'Mathematics or the Verifier?' is unsupported; the paper's own conclusion admits the second branch is open, so neither branch is answered.

Also (Null is uninformative about the verifier question because the recipe fails even with gold ): The paper's research question is 'Mathematics or the Verifier?', but it also reports that training on reference solutions does not improve the model and that accuracy falls at the highest rate in every run. A recipe that cannot improve with gold data is not a valid testbed for separating learning from verifier-fitting: the null is explained by the training setup (see the truncation/prompt-loss and low-capacity LoRA issues) and says nothing about verifier-filtered self-training. The paper concede

Also ('Null for the recipe' makes the headline contribution nearly empty: the recipe has no posi): Contribution 1 and the Conclusion scope the null to 'the recipe', but the recipe includes loss over the prompt, a 512-token training limit that includes the prompt, and 24-26% of the round-0 pool truncated so that it loses its final answer and end-of-sequence token (Section 3.4). Train-on-gold, the arm that should be the easiest win, drops 18-21 points. A pipeline in which supervised training on gold solutions destroys accuracy is not a test of whether verifier-filtered self-training can help, s

Also (Inference that the null 'concerns the recipe' rests on a train-on-gold arm run only at the): The argument that 'no arm improves, including training on reference solutions' shows the null may be a property of the recipe uses a gold arm that exists only at 5e-4, a rate at which every arm, including the filtered one, falls by 4-11 points and the gold arm by ~20 points while shifting style to $-delimited spans (5% -> 98%) and halving response length. Failing to improve at a destructive learning rate is weak evidence about whether the recipe can help at 1e-5 or 1e-4, where no gold arm was ru

title: Training setup truncates ~a quarter of the 'verified' pool and trains on the prompt
quote: loss over the whole chat sequence, prompt included
explanation:
Loss is computed on the prompt as well as the solution, and a 512-token limit that includes the prompt cuts 24-26% of the round-0 pool (62.4% in the no-filter arm) so that those examples lose their final answer and end-of-sequence token. Training on such truncated targets directly teaches the model to continue past 512 tokens without terminating, which is the cap-hit/finished-accuracy decline the paper later decomposes. The verifier accepted these solutions when generation was under 512 new tokens, so the problem is created by the paper's own mismatch between generation cap and training limit, not by the loop. Because this affects every arm, including train-on-gold, it confounds all null and decline claims and makes statements like 'accuracy falls at the highest rate' about this implementation rather than about GVT. Truncated examples should have been dropped or the limit raised, and the paper should state whether the tokenizer appends EOS for non-truncated examples.

Also (Training truncation strips the answer and EOS from a quarter of the 'verified' pool, so th): The verifier accepts a solution that finished within 512 generated tokens, but training uses a 512-token limit that also includes the prompt, so 24-26% of kept examples (62% with no filter) are cut and lose their final answer and end-of-sequence token. These examples are then trained as if they were correct, which teaches non-termination and answer-free continuations; this is a plausible direct cause of the observed rise in cap-hit and 'unfinished' generations, and it is a defect of the experime

title: Conditioning on the falling \boxed share removes the channel through which adaptation would appear
quote: the falling \boxed share is accounted for, but with about 25 aﬀected problems,
explanation:
The defect fires only on boxed predictions, so the only ways to escape it are to leave the answer unboxed or to change its form. The paper itself says "A model adapting to the defect would have to write these answers unboxed". A falling boxed share among correct answers is therefore the expected signature of adaptation, not an independent nuisance. Since r_all = (boxed share of V'-accepted) x r_boxed (my check: 15.7/20.7 = 0.76 and 18.3/20.0 = 0.92, matching the quoted 91 -> 76%), the 'all' fall is exactly the boxed-share fall, and the 'boxed only' row conditions on a post-treatment mediator. 'Flat once the boxed share is accounted for' then cannot distinguish 'no adaptation' from 'adaptation realised through dropping \boxed'. The paper's alternatives (imitation of a less-boxed pool, drift) are also unresolved, and the defect itself mildly selects against boxed answers in the V-filtered pool (V rejects ~18% of correct boxed answers and 0% of unboxed). No run without a verifier in the loop (the no-filter arm, the natural negative control) is in Table 4, so there is no benchmark for how far boxed share falls from drift alone. The Conclusion's wording 'finds no sign ... once the falling \boxed share is accounted for' presupposes the answer. The affected-problem subset is the only informative row, and its intervals (10-26 points wide) are uninformative. A difference-in-differences of boxed share on affected versus unaffected problems, plus a no-filter row, would address this.

Also (Falling \boxed share is treated as an alternative explanation to adaptation, but it is the): Section 5.3 concludes the fall in r_t is 'accounted for' by the falling \boxed share among correct answers, hence not adaptation. But the same section says adaptation to the gold-storage defect would consist precisely of writing answers unboxed (V' differs from V only on boxed predictions). Moreover the training pool is selected by V, which rejects boxed answers on defect-affected problems, so the pool is mechanically less boxed than the set of all correct answers; Section 4.4 attributes the fal

Also (Adaptation audit: an unexplained consistent fall in r_t is explained away post hoc, and th): In all three self-training runs r_t falls by 1.5-2.6 points with intervals that touch or just include zero, while train-on-gold shows a rise. The paper explains the fall by the declining \boxed share and then concludes 'no adaptation'. But \boxed share is itself an outcome of training (possibly caused by verifier-style learning: preferring formats the verifier accepts or not), so conditioning on it and reading the flat boxed-only r_t as a null is adjustment for a mediator, not a test. The hypoth

title: Adaptation audit is structurally unable to detect adaptation; 'flat' and 'no sign' are not evidence of absence
quote: It is bound to the problem, not to the
explanation:
The gold-storage defect is described as bound to the problem and rejecting 94-98% of correct answers on the 54-62 problems where it fires, with 29-34 of them having a gold V cannot parse so that 'no answer form avoids it'. In offline SFT a problem whose correct answers are always rejected never contributes a training example, and the model cannot change any answer form that would escape the rejection. There is therefore no selection pressure or gradient that could teach the model to 'avoid' this defect, and a flat or slowly falling r_t is the expected outcome whether or not the model is verifier-sensitive. The audit thus has not just 'low power' (as the paper concedes) but no possible positive outcome on those problems; the 'no adaptation' conclusion in the abstract and contributions is nearly vacuous. Only the 24-28 problems with an escaping form can carry information, and the pool there is 2-12 examples per round. The paper should either drop the 'we find no adaptation' framing or build a positive control (e.g. inject a bias with an escaping form).

Also (The audit as run is structurally unable to find adaptation, yet is presented as a general ): The unconditional prediction is contradicted by the paper's own analysis. Under SFT, boxed correct answers on affected problems are rejected 94-98% of the time, so they never enter the pool and carry no negative gradient; the only 'teaching' signal is 2-12 accepted examples per round out of 330-440. Table 4 shows the pool is largest (9-12) in the 10^-5 run, where the adapter barely changes outputs (section 4.2), and smallest (2-5) at 5e-4 where the model changes most. Pressure and capacity to ad

Also ('Flat' boxed-only r_t is not evidence of absence; intervals are as wide as the effects int): Table 4's boxed-only intervals are [-2.9, 4.3], [-2.8, 3.4] and [-2.0, 1.2], which contain the full 'all' decline of -2.6 and also -5 points. 'Flat' describes point estimates; with no equivalence margin, a true effect as large as the one being explained away is compatible with the data. Also, the three 'all' falls (-2.6, -2.6, -1.5) are all negative, with upper limits of 0.3, 0.1 and 0.0, i.e. consistent in sign across three runs, which the paper dismisses by the boxed-share argument only. Furth

Also (Contribution 2 states the affected-problem r_t is 'flat' although Table 4 shows a -5.5 poi): Table 4's affected, parseable rows move by -5.5 [-20.1, 6.3], -1.6 [-14.7, 9.5] and -0.2 [-4.9, 4.6]. Intervals of 10-26 points wide cannot establish 'flat'; the largest estimated change is the one the authors would expect under adaptation, and the text of 5.3 itself says 'moves by -5.5, -1.6 and -0.2'. Beyond wording, the contribution is an audit with no positive control (no run where adaptation is known to occur), a related-work section that says the measurement 'is not new either' (per-step t

title: Detectable-effect and 2.2-point bound are post hoc, omit seed variance and conflict with the paper's own noise
quote: 5% level only if it exceeded about 2.8 h/1.96: about 10 points of pass@1, 8–10
explanation:
The design detects only about 10 points of pass@1 (and 3.5-5.5 of sample accuracy), larger than typical gains of rejection-sampling SFT at this scale, so a 'null' is compatible with all realistic effects. The MDE is computed from observed interval half-widths of the same runs (a post hoc power analysis), and the paper itself notes the intervals do not include training-seed variance (the replicate pair differs by 3.2 points of sample accuracy, comparable to the MDE). The quoted '2.2-point bound' on sample-accuracy gains is both post hoc in the choice of measure and smaller than the stated 3.5-5.5 MDE for the same measure, which makes the two statements hard to reconcile for a reader: the 2.2 bound is a confidence limit, the MDE is a power statement, and neither accounts for seed noise. No equivalence/non-inferiority test or pre-specified margin is used, so 'no detectable gain' is an absence-of-evidence statement; the paper also admits no multiplicity correction while concluding from patterns over many intervals. The paper applies a laxer standard to its own claims than the rigour it asks of the RLVR literature in the Introduction.

Also (Detectable-effect figures rest on bootstrap half-widths that the paper's own data show are): The 80%-power threshold 2.8*h/1.96 (correct for a two-sided 5% test: 1.96+0.84) is built from the half-widths h of within-run problem-level bootstrap intervals, which by the paper's own statement exclude training-seed variance. The paper's evidence says this variance is not small: the replicate pair ends 3.2 points of sample accuracy apart, and Section 4.4 reports a same-pool-size B minus A pass@1 difference of -7.3 [-14.0, -0.7] at seed 2 whose interval excludes zero, which is then called 'traj

Also (MDE rule 2.8h/1.96 is observed-power from post hoc intervals and yields an uninformative n): The minimum detectable effect is back-computed from the half-widths of intervals the experiments themselves produced (observed/retrospective power), averaged over runs and measures. It is correct arithmetically (1.96+0.84=2.8 times the SE) but only for the problem-bootstrap SE: it excludes training-seed variance (the one replicate pair differs by 3.2 points, larger than the claimed 3.5-5.5 sample-accuracy MDE would tolerate as noise-free), so the true MDE is larger. The stated MDE (about 10 pass

Also (Quoted MDE ranges only roughly reproduce from Table 2 half-widths (controls and k=4/k=8 mi): Recomputing 1.43*h from Table 2 (h = half-width): pass@1 gives 8.6-10.5 for the self-training rows but 11.9 for Gold,1 (h=8.35); pass@k gives 8.6-10.4 (11.4 for Gold); sample accuracy gives 3.4-3.8 for the four 10^-5 rows (k=8), 4.6-5.4 for 10^-4/2x10^-4 and 5.0-5.7 for 5x10^-4 (k=4), and 7.1-7.9 for the two Gold rows. So '3.5-5.5' is really 3.4-5.7 excluding Gold and the lower end applies only to the k=8, 10^-5 runs; the k=4 rates, which carry the main decline claims, have MDE about 4.6-5.7. Sa

Also (The 2.2-point bound on gains is smaller than the acknowledged seed noise and is a maximum ): I recomputed from Table 2: the largest upper limit of a sample-accuracy interval over all 17 rows is +2.2 (A,1 and A,3 at 10^-4). Reading this as 'the data exclude gains above 2.2' conflicts with Section 3.4, which says the same intervals imply a design able to detect only 3.5-5.5 points, and with the 3.2-point gap between the two replicates (larger than the bound itself). An interval upper limit equals the (negative) point estimate plus h, so it is small largely because runs drifted down; it sa

Also (The 2.2-point bound is a post hoc maximum of observed upper limits, smaller than the paper): The bound is the largest upper end among per-run bootstrap intervals (Table 2: +2.2 for A seed 3 at 1e-4 and A seed 1 at 1e-4), on a measure chosen after the runs, with no equivalence margin fixed in advance. Section 3.4 says the only replicate pair ends 3.2 points apart in sample accuracy, which is larger than the bound itself, so seed variance alone could move a run by more than the 'excluded' gain; the bound therefore says little about what the recipe can do. It also sits uneasily beside the 

Also (2.2-point exclusion bound sits uneasily with the quoted 3.5-5.5 detectable effect and the ): The 2.2 comes from the largest upper ends in Table 2 (+2.2 for A,1 and A,3 at 10^-4); every other MATH-500 row is lower. But those rows are k=4 runs whose half-widths (3.3-3.9) imply an MDE of about 4.6-5.6 by the paper's own 2.8h/1.96 rule, and the abstract/intro/conclusion present both '3.5-5.5 could have been missed' and 'gains above 2.2 excluded' without reconciling them: the bound is small only because the point estimates are negative (-1.0 to -3.7), not because the design is precise. Add t

Also (The 2.2-point 'exclusion of gains' is a one-sided CI artifact that conflicts with the pape): The 2.2 figure is the largest upper end among observed intervals, and those upper ends are small only because the observed point estimates are negative (e.g. [-5.3, 2.2] around -1.5). It is not a statement about the design's sensitivity: the same section says the design can only detect 3.5-5.5 points of sample accuracy, and the two numbers are not reconciled. The interval omits training-seed variance, and the paper's own replicate pair ends 3.2 points apart, which exceeds the bound it is used to

Also ('Replicate pair 3.2 points apart' matches no pair in Tables 1-2 and understates same-seed ): No same-configuration pair in Table 2 differs by 3.2 on sample accuracy: A,0 vs A,1 at 10^-5 are -2.4 vs -1.5 (0.9); B,0 vs B,1 are -3.2 vs -1.2 (2.0); 10^-4 seeds range -1.0 to -3.7 (2.7); the 5x10^-4 A seeds are -8.3 vs -4.7 (3.6). Moreover the paper treats same-seed A/B as near-replicates (Sec 4.4), and at 5x10^-4 seed 2 A and B differ by 4.5 points of sample accuracy (-4.7 vs -9.2; 7.3 points of pass@1), larger than the 3.2 'the one replicate pair'. Identify which pair gives 3.2 and note tha

title: Learning-rate and arm comparisons are confounded by dose, k, rounds, pool size and truncation; 'any learning rate' overstated
quote: detect no improvement on held-out problems at any learning rate we tried, but
explanation:
The research question is about 'several' GVT rounds, but all 1e-4 to 5e-4 runs have three rounds, i.e. two adapters, and the round-2 model is one adapter trained on the round-1 pool (Sec 3.3). Because adapters restart from base, earlier rounds cannot compound, so the design cannot test cumulative improvement at all (Sec 3.1 admits it gives compounding less room). The 1e-5 arm (5 rounds, k=8) is reported to change outputs little, and the other rates change k, rounds and pool size at once (Limitations), so the 'grid' is not a sweep of one variable; the paper itself says only the comparison among 1e-4, 2e-4 and 5e-4 isolates the rate. GSM8K appears with one seed at 1e-5 and one run at 5e-4, and the stated MDE (about 10/8-10/3.5-5.5) is computed from MATH-500 intervals only, so 'no detectable gain' on GSM8K has no stated sensitivity. The abstract thus compresses a sparse, confounded design into 'at [K] learning rates on MATH-500 and GSM8K'. Not wrong, but the strongest accurate statement is much narrower: no gain larger than ~3-10 points at 3 rounds with restart-from-base on MATH-500.

Also (Learning-rate, k and round choices were post hoc, started from an untuned (too-low) defaul): The first Design I grid used 1e-5 for LoRA, an untuned default that the authors then found 'changed the MATH-500 outputs little', so the entire five-round k=8 study is close to uninformative about training effects (and its null at 1e-5 is largely a statement about a near-no-op adapter). Higher rates, three rounds and k=4 were then chosen after observing results. The grid only moves upward and never explores the 'sweet spot' region below 1e-4 or other recipes (more epochs, full-linear targets), a

Also (Learning-rate comparisons change k, rounds, pool size and metric simultaneously): The 1e-5 runs (k=8, five rounds, pass@8 as pass@k, last round R4) and the higher-rate runs (k=4, three rounds, pass@4, last round R2) differ in four factors besides the rate, so no statement about how the effect depends on learning rate can use the 1e-5 row; only the 1e-4/2e-4/5e-4 rows are comparable. Yet Table 2 lists them together under a single 'Change from round 0 to the last round', the MDEs are pooled across them (pass@1 is a single draw at either k), and pass@k means different things at 

Also (Controls and arms differ in dose, so no cross-arm comparison is interpretable): The no-filter arm uses 3-4x the optimizer steps of Run A (1,400 vs 326-440 examples), is truncated 62.4% vs 24.5%, and the train-on-gold arm uses 350 human-written reference solutions of a different length, style and distribution (responses shorten by more than half, $-delimited spans 5% to 98%). Thus 'no-filter is not better than filtered', 'gold is much worse', 'patch has no effect', and the verifier-vs-no-verifier question are each confounded by dose, truncation and style shift. The paper adm

Also (Learning rate 1e-5 with q/v LoRA is far outside the usual regime; 'at any learning rate' i): The main five-round, k=8 runs use LR 1e-5 for rank-16 LoRA on q_proj and v_proj only, an untuned default; LoRA typically needs 1e-4 to 2e-4 or higher, and the paper itself admits the adapter 'did little' and the 10^-5 patch control is uninformative. The higher-LR runs then change k (4), rounds (3, i.e. two adapters) and pool size at the same time, and the 5e-4 runs already degrade. The abstract and intro's 'at any learning rate we tried' therefore rests on a very coarse grid where the useful win

Also ('Several rounds' framing vs. at most two adapters in the main evidence): The research question concerns compounding over 'several GVT rounds', but each round trains a fresh adapter from the base on only the previous round's pool, and most of the later evidence (3 rounds at k=4) has just two adapters, with the round-2 model a single adapter trained on the round-1 pool. This design gives compounding, the key feature of iterated self-improvement (and of ReST-EM-style results the paper cites), little room, as the paper itself admits in 3.1 but not in the Introduction, Ab

title: Bootstrap ignores training-seed variance; same-seed arms treated as independent; no multiplicity control
quote: These intervals do not cover training-seed variance, which we see only
explanation:
The bootstrap resamples 150 problems with the trained adapters fixed, so it quantifies exam-sampling noise only. The training pipeline (data order, LoRA init, sampled pool) is a second, large noise source. The paper itself supplies evidence that it matters: A vs B differ by a patch that changes 0-3 training examples, yet B-A in round-2 pass@1 is +5.3 at seed 1 and -7.3 [-14.0, -0.7] at seed 2, an interval excluding zero for what is effectively an A/A contrast. This is a direct false-positive of the CI procedure and shows the nominal 95% coverage is not attained for run-to-run comparisons. The paper notes 'trajectory noise' but still reads individual intervals (e.g. 'only just exclude zero for A and B at seed 0') as signals, and builds its 'detectable effect' on them. Seed count is 1-3 per condition, so seed variance cannot be estimated reliably either.

Also (Same-seed A/B arms and shared round-0 baselines are counted as independent runs): Runs at one seed share the exam partition, the selection set, the round-0 model and its single set of round-0 samples, so every arm's 'change' is measured against the same baseline draw (e.g. seed 1 round 0 sample accuracy is 33.7 in every row). A high or low baseline realisation then moves all arms' deltas together, and regression to the mean can make 'every run declines' partly one baseline artifact. The paper concedes A/B are 'closer to two replicates than four' but continues to tally them ('

Also (No multiplicity control and asymmetric reading of intervals; consistent negative direction): Table 2 reports roughly 17 rows x 4 measures of intervals with no correction, and the text then selects which to emphasise. Intervals containing zero are read as 'no gain' and, at the same time, a 'possible small decline, not an established one'; intervals excluding zero for declines at 5e-4 are treated as real. The honest finding of Table 2 is directional: all sample-accuracy changes are negative (-1.0 to -19.7), and at 1e-5 to 2e-4 all 11 are negative with nearly all point estimates -1 to -4.

title: Consistent negative direction at 1e-5 is read as 'no detectable change'
quote: We read this as a possible small decline, not an established
explanation: In Table 2 the sample-accuracy change is negative in every A/B row on MATH-500 (all 11 rows at 10^-5 to 5e-4, excluding controls) and pass@1 is negative in all but one (A,1 at 10^-4 is +0.7); at 10^-5 all four runs fall 1.2-3.2 points of sample accuracy and 2.7-4.0 of pass@1, with matched finished accuracy falling in all four. Section 3.4 says conclusions should rest on 'patterns across runs and seeds, not on single intervals', but here the pattern (a uniform sign across runs) is discounted run by run because each interval touches zero. The same section then argues that a flat output-length/cap-hit curve is 'weak evidence that the adapter did little', which sits uneasily with a consistent accuracy decline of 1-4 points that the adapter must have caused (round 0 is the same base model). Either the decline is real (a small harm even at 10^-5) or there is a systematic round-0 vs later-round difference (e.g. sampling or scoring), and the paper should say which and pool the runs (e.g. a sign test or pooled paired estimate over A/B/seed) rather than leave the pattern unevaluated. The A/B pairs are close to replicates, so the effective number of independent runs is small, which is also worth stating.

title: Primary measure (sample accuracy) chosen after seeing results
quote: so after the runs we chose it as the primary
explanation: The pre-set measures (pass@1, pass@k) had wide intervals (half-widths ~6-7 points) that cannot exclude anything useful; sample accuracy, chosen after the runs because its intervals are tighter, is now the measure on which the tightest claims (the 2.2-point bound, 'sample-accuracy intervals exclude zero in all four A/B runs', the decomposition into finished accuracy and cap share) are built. Choosing the metric after outcomes is a degree-of-freedom that can only produce more 'significant' declines and narrower bounds, and the direction of effects is the same sign-selected data. The paper discloses this, but the abstract and conclusion still mix pre-set and post hoc measures, and the pre-set pass@1 rule is declared 'one-sided' only in hindsight, so no hypothesis in the paper was truly confirmatory. Sample accuracy also conflates correctness with termination (41-48% of base generations hit the cap), so it is not 'the same quantity' as pass@1 for this model.

title: Verifier manipulation has essentially no dose; 'verifier bias' is the authors' own storage bug
quote: The gold-storage defect (post hoc).
explanation:
The title, abstract and intro ask whether the model learned 'what the verifier accepts', citing verifier false negatives from TinyV, Huang et al. and Egashira et al. But the only frequent defect (about one in six correct solutions; 15.5-18.4%) is a data-storage bug in this pipeline (gold stored without delimiters), discovered post hoc and never varied; the genuine math-verify parser defect (\dfrac, 0-4 examples) is rare. The audit therefore measures adaptation to an engineering error that a correctly configured math-verify call would not have, which limits relevance to the cited RLVR literature (where verifiers are used as intended) and makes the claim of studying 'verifier bias' largely a claim about a self-inflicted artifact. The related-work positioning ('applied to ... a defect of our own pipeline') concedes this but title and contributions do not.

Also (The verifier manipulation, the title's key variable, has essentially no dose): The only treatment that varies the verifier is the \dfrac patch (0-4 of ~440 examples, under 0.5%), the no-filter arm removes the verifier but adds 3-4x dose, and the frequent gold-storage defect was never varied. Hence the paper has no experiment in which verifier bias is the manipulated factor with a measurable difference in the training data. The question in the title cannot be answered with that design, and the post hoc dose analysis (check iii) arrives only after the runs. 'No difference be

Also (Claimed '\dfrac/\tfrac rejected 100%' may be an artifact of the same storage defect): math-verify is designed to parse \dfrac and \tfrac when they appear in $...$ or \boxed{}. A probe that is 'rejected 100% of the time' for a command the library is known to handle suggests the probe (or the pipeline) supplies the answer without a delimiter, i.e. it is the same missing-delimiter gold-storage defect, not a separate verifier weakness. If so, the 'patch' control and the 'rarer defect' narrative in the abstract are mis-specified: the patch repairs a symptom of the defect it leaves in 

Also (Claim that false rejects 'only remove a training example' is at odds with the paper's own ): The Introduction justifies the SFT setting by saying a false reject only removes an example, implying lower stakes than RLVR. But a systematic false reject removes whole answer forms and whole problems from the pool (the paper's own 54-62 problems with 94-98% rejection), so SFT learns from a pool skewed toward parseable gold forms; this is the same directional bias the paper claims to study. The 'cheapest and most widely used form of the loop' is also asserted without citation. The contrast with

title: Defect-bound problems and unparsable golds are treated as a harmless constant offset
quote: That is a constant oﬀset in counts within a partition, so it cancels in within-run
explanation: The 51 unparsable golds (10.2%) and the 54-62 defect problems are said to cancel in within-run differences. That holds for the count of solved problems only if those problems are never solved by any arm. But they also never enter the training pool, so every pool is systematically restricted to problems with simple, parseable gold forms (the defect-free problems), and the V-vs-V' re-scoring shows the effect is not constant (original-verifier changes are 0.73-0.85 of re-scored ones). This is exactly the 'directional verifier bias' the paper's title is about, acting on the training distribution, yet the Setup reduces it to an additive offset. The text also does not say whether exam problems with unparsable gold are excluded from the denominator of pass rates, which determines whether the 'cancels' argument applies to levels and relative effects.

title: Verifier error audit (7.8% FN) and V' are small, other-model-sourced and unvalidated
quote: the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128; Wilson interval
explanation: The 7.8% estimate comes from solutions of a different, larger model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) rather than the 1.5B policy, from 200 problems, with 'correct' defined by a scripted normalised comparison whose own error rate is not reported; the 128 judged-correct subset is not explained. The conclusion that 'most are compound answers, so probably largely the gold-storage defect' is speculation. More importantly, the paper builds r_t (and the headline 'one in six') on V', a verifier that wraps the gold in \boxed{} when the prediction contains a box, yet the text admits the audit gives no false-positive rate and V' is never validated against a human or independent judge. If V' accepts wrong answers that V rightly rejects, r_t and its 15.5-18.4% overstate the defect. Predictions without a box are handled by an unspecified rule.

title: Possible base-model contamination and exam reuse undermine 'held-out' and 'mathematics' claims
quote: the ﬁrst 500 problems of the GSM8K test
explanation:
Qwen2.5 models are known to have substantial exposure to MATH and GSM8K-style data, and the paper itself cites Shao et al. for random-reward gains from pre-existing behaviour. Using the first 500 GSM8K test problems and MATH-500 with a 150-problem exam, with no contamination check or fresh held-out set, undermines the claim that a held-out exam measures new learning rather than verifier-style or memorised behaviour; the same applies when the exam is only 150 problems and the pool 350 problems from the same distribution.

Also (Test-set contamination of the base model is relegated to a three-word limitation yet bears): MATH-500 is a subset of the MATH test split and GSM8K test is a standard benchmark; Qwen2.5-Instruct models are widely suspected to have seen their training distributions and possibly benchmark items. The 'held-out exam' is held out only from the GVT loop, not from the model's pretraining/post-training, so (i) the base accuracy and ceiling may reflect memorisation, which would make any further gain hard to find and make declines look like disruption of memorised recall; (ii) the train-on-gold ar

Also ('Held-out exam' and 'mathematics' claims rest on a verifier-graded, possibly contaminated,): The first research question is whether the model gets better at mathematics, but every accuracy number is graded by V (Limitations: 'Every headline number is graded by the biased veriﬁer that also selects the data'), 51/500 golds are unparsable (11-18 of 150 exam problems always count as unsolved), and the gold-storage defect lowers pass@1 by 4.7-8.0 points. The paper notes that original-verifier changes are 0.73-0.85 of the re-scored ones but declines to rescale; applied, that means a V-measure

Also (The exam is reused for design decisions and verifier diagnosis, and exam sets rotate acros): The 150-problem exam is a single small set per seed, yet it has been used to choose the learning rates, k, number of rounds, primary measure and to diagnose the verifier (the defect audit and V' are computed on all 500 problems, including exam and selection items, and the gold-storage defect was found by inspecting generations). Hence exam results are not clean held-out estimates for the later analysis choices. In addition, with partitions drawn from the same 500 problems, an exam problem at one

title: 'Pooled collapse does not reproduce' is not a replication and conflicts with Run C
quote: a pooled design whose sharp decline did not reproduce under
explanation:
The Intro presents the Design P collapse as a reading that 'did not hold up' under isolation, but P and I differ in model mix (0.5B and 1.5B), pooling of two datasets in one adapter, 4.5x larger pools, k, scoring on selection problems (train-on-eval) rather than a held-out exam, and learning rate/step counts (Design P training logs were not saved). Section 4.1 admits no run separates these explanations, so neither 'did not reproduce' nor 'does not hold up' is justified; the correct statement is that the two designs are not comparable. Because P evaluates on its own selection set, its pass rates are also not comparable to I's exam numbers, and the pooled collapse is an unexplained, un-diagnosed result that could equally reflect a pipeline bug (e.g. the truncation issue), which would also affect Design I.

Also ('Pooled collapse does not reproduce under isolation' conflicts with large isolated decline): Intro and Conclusion state flatly that the sharp pooled decline 'did not reproduce under isolation', but (a) Section 4.2 reports Run C (GSM8K, isolated, 1e-5) falling 12.7 pass@1 points with an interval excluding zero, and Run C at 5e-4 falling 22.0; (b) the high-rate MATH runs fall 4-11 points and train-on-gold falls ~20; (c) Section 5.1 concedes that pooling, selection-set scoring and dose (4.5x more examples) were confounded and 'we cannot say' which produced the pooled curve. A failure to re

title: Train-on-gold r_t explanation ('more boxed') contradicts Table 4; verifier-error argument is a non sequitur
quote: as its outputs become more boxed, a reminder that rt moves with format for
explanation:
The text attributes the +2.1 to +3.3 rise in r_t for train-on-gold to outputs becoming more boxed. But Table 4's 'boxed only' rows, which by construction remove the boxed-share effect, rise by nearly the same amount (+2.8 and +1.7). Recomputing the boxed share from r_all/r_boxed gives 18.2/20.0 = 0.91 -> 21.5/22.8 = 0.94 and 18.0/19.4 = 0.93 -> 20.2/21.1 = 0.96, a ~3-point change worth about 0.6 points of r_t, i.e. a small part of the rise. Most of the rise is thus a boxed-only effect that the 'boxed share' explanation does not cover (section 4.4 also reports that gold-trained outputs switch to $-delimited spans, 5% -> 98%, a different format change). This matters because the same device ('the fall is explained by boxed share') is used to dismiss the -1.5 to -2.6 point falls in the self-training rows. It also shows r_t moves by +/-3 points from format effects of unknown origin, which is the same size as the effects being interpreted, so the audit has no demonstrated noise floor.

Also (Verifier-error argument for train-on-gold is a non sequitur): The text says post hoc checks 'bound verifier error from below only (about 2 points ...)' and that 14% of round-2 generations without \boxed are not covered, and then concludes 'we think this fall is unlikely to be mainly verifier error'. A lower bound of about 2 points on verifier error cannot support a claim that verifier error is small relative to a 20-point fall; the paper itself says it 'cannot bound it from above'. The risk is concrete: train-on-gold moves the output style to the reference

title: Cap-share decomposition is underspecified, unstable, and the 1,536-token evidence uses the discredited proxy
quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1 runs
explanation:
The 'three-part decomposition' is not defined in the main text (no formula, no statement of what accuracy is assigned to cap-hit generations, no order or interaction handling), so the 12-30% and 52-72% figures cannot be reproduced from Table 1/2. As a rough check, with Table 1 the cap-hit share rises ~3 points at seed 1 (decline 8.4) and ~8 points at seed 2 (decline 4.6); depending on the accuracy assigned to capped samples, the seed-2 share could be anywhere from ~50% to ~90%, so the result is sensitive to unstated choices. The figures are ratios whose denominators are themselves uncertain (A seed 2 sample-accuracy change [-8.2, -1.2]), reported without intervals, and some are negative or near zero (-2% and 5%). Seed and exam partition are not separable (each seed has its own partition), yet 5.3(ii) says 'its balance differs by partition' and the Conclusion draws a seed-level contrast ('clearly only at one of its two seeds') from two runs with a shared design. The Table 2 'finished, matched' column is on a different scale (conditional on finishing, ~half the samples) from 'sample acc.' and can exceed it (A seed 2: -5.5 vs -4.7), which is easy to misread as exceeding the total decline.

Also (Decomposition percentages (12-30% seed 1, 52-72% seed 2) cannot be reproduced from main-te): Rough check with Table 1 (cap-hit R0 43.0-43.2% vs R2 46.2% at seed 1, 51.2% at seed 2) and sample accuracy (A: 33.7 -> 25.3 at seed 1, 30.8 -> 26.2 at seed 2): treating cap-hit generations as wrong, the cap part is about 1.8 of 8.4 points (about 21%) at seed 1, consistent with 12-30%, but about 4.3 of 4.6 points (above 90%) for A at seed 2, outside 52-72%. Using the matched-finished column instead (-9.1 and -5.5, scaled by the finished share) gives roughly 40% cap at both seeds. The paper does 

Also (1,536-token evidence relies on the character proxy that the same section calls unreliable,): Section 4.5 states that the earlier character-length proxy 'overstated termination' because drifting prose crosses its threshold within the same token budget, and section 3.4 states the per-sample outputs of the 1,536-token re-scorings were not saved, so token-based cap-hit cannot be recomputed. The sentence nevertheless uses that proxy to conclude that the remaining deficit comes from generations that do not stop. Two problems follow: (a) the inference relies on the measure shown to be biased,

title: Table 4 omits the no-filter control that would calibrate r_t
quote: Train-on-gold, with no veriﬁer in the loop, gives rt rises of 2.1–3.3 points
explanation: The only 'negative' reference for r_t is train-on-gold, a run that changes style drastically (shorter responses, $-delimited spans) and collapses accuracy, hence poorly matched to the self-training arms. The no-filter arm (verifier removed, similar sampling distribution, same learning rate, two seeds) is the natural comparison: if r_t and boxed share fall as much there as in the filtered arms, the falls are drift. If they fall less, selection by V contributes. The paper has the generations (they are saved) and reports no-filter results elsewhere, yet Table 4 and the text do not include it, leaving the key attribution (selection by V vs drift vs imitation) untested even descriptively. This is also needed to interpret the Conclusion's statement that the boxed-share fall is consistent with both imitation and drift.

title: Finished-accuracy headline mixes arms; 'removing the filter is never better' not supported by tables
quote: generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same
explanation:
The range quoted in Contribution 3 and the Conclusion comes from six 5e-4 runs including the two no-filter arms (Table 2: A seed 1 -9.1, A seed 2 -5.5 [-11.7, 0.1], B seed 1 -6.8, B seed 2 -5.9, no-filter -10.6 and -6.6). The lower end, 5.5, belongs to a run whose interval includes zero (4.5 admits 'five of six'), and two pairs are same-seed A/B near-replicates, so the effective number of independent observations is about four. The matched measure also 'conditions on which problems finish after training' and is described as descriptive, yet is worded causally ('lose'). Combined with the sentence that cap-share accounts for 12-30% of the decline at seed 1 but 52-72% at seed 2 (a spread that undermines any single decomposition claim), the contribution reads as a stable quantitative finding while the text calls it descriptive and partly known (Xu et al. already identify the fixed-token-cap failure the paper cites as closest work). The decomposition is therefore a modest methodological note rather than an independent contribution of equal standing to the others.

Also (Intro contribution quotes 5.5-10.6 'at the highest rate' but omits Gold and Run C, which T): The 5.5-10.6 range covers A, B and no-filter at 5x10^-4 (six runs, Table 2 matched column). At the same rate Table 2 also lists Gold (-25.6, -25.9) and Run C (-12.1), outside this range; Sec 4.5 handles Gold separately ('Train-on-gold is different') but the intro, conclusion and Summary state it as a property of 'the highest rate' without the restriction. Add 'in the verifier-filtered and no-filter MATH-500 runs'.

Also ('Removing the filter is never better' is not what Tables 2-3 show, and it undercuts the ve): Table 3 seed 1 round 2: no-filter pass@1 27.3 vs verifier-filtered 23.3 (no-filter is better); Table 2 seed 1: no-filter delta pass@1 -6.0 vs A -10.0 and sample accuracy -8.2 vs -8.3, while seed 2 goes the other way (-10.2 vs -4.7). The accurate statement is that the two arms are indistinguishable with a sign that flips by seed and measure. This matters substantively: if training on all unfiltered samples at 3-4x dose does as badly as, or no worse than, verifier-filtered training, the data canno

Also ('Worse on pass@4 at both seeds' stated although intervals include zero and one difference ): The no-filter minus A round-2 pass@4 differences are -2.0 (3 of 150 problems) and about -5.3, both with intervals that include zero by the paper's own account. Calling the control 'worse' at both seeds is directional language that the evidence does not support under the paper's own standard (no conclusions from single intervals). Table 3 also shows no-filter pass@1 above A at seed 2 in round 1 (34.7 vs 31.3). The sentence is hedged by the dose caveat, but 'never better ... and is worse' should r

title: Measurement ceiling: 512 cap, unparsable golds and defective verifier limit what any test can see
quote: The untrained model already hits the cap in 41–48% of MATH-500 generations,
explanation: The instrument that must detect a gain is itself damaged. Nearly half of base generations are cut at 512 tokens, 10.2% of golds are unparsable and count as always unsolved (11-18 per 150-problem exam, i.e. 7-12% of the exam), and the gold-storage defect rejects 15-18% of correct boxed answers (94-98% on 54-62 problems). Part of the possible gain from self-training (shorter, terminating solutions, boxing) is thus blocked by the pipeline, and the headroom varies by partition so 'constant offset' arguments hold only within partition. Because this is the evaluation of the very effect being tested, 'no detectable gain' says as much about the benchmark pipeline as about the training method. The paper does not report the same experiments scored with a repaired verifier and a non-binding token cap for the main table (only partial re-scorings), so the primary null is not shown to survive removal of these ceilings.

title: Audit and cap decomposition listed as contributions despite being non-novel, post hoc and unvalidated; novelty claims too broad
quote: A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one veriﬁer defect, carried over
explanation:
Contribution 2 (and the abstract, Section 5.3 title 'A Proposed Audit', and the Conclusion) frame the false-reject audit as a deliverable, yet the paper itself says in Related Work that 'The per-round false-reject measurement of Section 5.3 is not new either: it is the per-step tracking of Egashira et al. and TinyV', that all four checks 'were deﬁned post hoc' and are offered 'not as tested methods', and the Limitations state 'no positive control'. The result is a null (rt falls 1.5-2.6 points with intervals touching zero, explained by a falling \boxed share), so the audit has never been shown able to detect adaptation when it exists. A protocol whose sensitivity is unknown cannot be listed as a finding or contribution; the only transferable novelty is the observation that rt must be conditioned on answer format, which is a caveat, not a validated method. The Conclusion's 'natural next step' (apply to public RLVR checkpoints) was not done. Recommend demoting it to a discussion/future-work item or adding a positive control (e.g. train on V-only-accepted data and show rt falls).

Also (Closest prior work (Xu et al., Phantom Gains) overlaps two of three contributions; differe): Xu et al. [15] already audit LoRA self-training against a frozen control, find measurement failures including fixed-token-cap under style drift and training-seed variance. The paper says this is the reason for its Contribution 3 (decomposing accuracy into finished-accuracy and cap-share), so that contribution is a re-application of a known failure mode, and a decomposition of this kind is elementary arithmetic rather than a new method. Contribution 1 (a null for self-training at a different scal

Also (Novelty claim 'None measures...' may be satisfied by cited verifier-error work): Related Work asserts that STaR/ReST/ReST-EM/RFT do not measure how the filter's errors depend on answer form, and later cites TinyV and Egashira et al. for verifier error. TinyV characterises false negatives by type (formatting, symbolic/format variants of the same answer) and Egashira et al. study systematic vs random false negatives in RLVR; both are measurements of how the verifier's errors depend on answer form, which the paper's own Section 3.2 format probe repeats. The statement is also co

Also (Over-broad novelty statement that no prior self-training work studies filter errors by ans): The sentence is stated flatly about STaR, ReST, ReST-EM and RFT, while the next paragraphs cite TinyV (rule-based verifiers reject correct solutions), Huang et al. (verifier recall) and Egashira et al. (systematic false negatives), which do measure how a rule-based verifier's rejections depend on the answer's form. The paper's own evidence for the form dependence is small (10 of 128 false negatives, \dfrac probe). The claim also compares the wrong sets: those four methods used ground-truth answe

title: Cited findings stated inconsistently (Wang, Shao, Egashira, Kim) and reference naming/IDs need checking
quote: Wang et al. separate out format correction and report only 8.6 of their 37.6 points as lying beyond it, but the studies mostly do not ask what the rest consists of.
explanation:
In the Introduction the numbers are tied to [14] ('from 36.0% to 73.6% on MATH-500 [14], a gain whose authors report only 8.6 points beyond format correction'); in Related Work the 8.6/37.6 claim appears with a bare author name and no [14], and 37.6 is never derived (it equals 73.6 - 36.0 only if the reader computes it). No table or section of Wang et al. is given for the 8.6 figure, so a reader cannot check that it is a MATH-500 number for the same model and not, say, an average or different setting. The sentence also uses Wang et al. as an example of a study that does ask the question while concluding that 'the studies mostly do not', which muddles whether the paper is building on or departing from this work. Note too that the 8.6 figure is about format correction, not about verifier-specific learning, so it supports the paper's motivation only indirectly. Cite [14] at each use, state the quantity once, and give a locator.

Also (Shao et al. comparison juxtaposed with Wang et al. without matching model/setting, then us): The Introduction places Shao et al.'s 7B result right after Wang et al.'s 1.5B result with 'Yet', as if they conflict, but they involve different models, different reward conditions and different baselines; Shao et al. themselves note that the spurious-reward effect is largely specific to Qwen2.5-Math (the Related Work admits 'the eﬀect varies by model family'). This is stated in Related Work but not in the Introduction, where the 21.4/29.1 figures are used to suggest that a rising score may ref

Also (Egashira et al. findings stated inconsistently and 'harmless' overstates a paper titled 'D): Related Work says Egashira et al. 'ﬁnd in RLVR that systematic false negatives behave like random noise', and the cited title lists 'Delay' as one outcome, i.e. false negatives slow learning rather than being harmless. Section 5.2 then says they find them 'harmless', and Section 5.3 and the Introduction attribute to them the per-step tracking and the 'unlearns the behaviour' observation. Each is a different strength of claim about [4], without number in Sections 4-5 ('Egashira et al.' with no ma

Also (Kim et al. analogy mismatches the paper's train-on-gold control): Kim et al.'s title concerns self-distillation degrading reasoning (the student is trained on its own or a conditioned teacher's outputs). The paper's train-on-gold arm is plain SFT on reference solutions with loss over the prompt and a 512-token training limit that truncates a quarter of the pool, so its accuracy drop and shorter outputs have many simpler explanations (distribution shift from terse MATH solutions, prompt-loss training, truncation). Calling this 'a similar surface signature' impl

Also (Citation naming style inconsistent; 'Imperfect Verifiers [1]' and 'From Accuracy to Robust): Reference 1 is titled 'Reinforcement Learning with Veriﬁable yet Noisy Rewards under Imperfect Veriﬁers' (Cai et al.), so the text uses an invented short title in place of a name, whereas [6] is cited by its (full) title fragment, [16] by 'TinyV', and [4], [14], [15], [9], [7] by 'X et al.'. A reader cannot tell that 'Imperfect Veriﬁers' is Cai et al. Cai et al. is also a relevant, closely related paper (noisy rewards with asymmetric false-positive and false-negative rates, with a correction met

Also (Several 2026 references cannot be verified from the reference list; two carry load in the ): Reference 15 (arXiv:2608.20290), 4 (2605.02909), 7 (2603.24472), 8 (2606.13732) and 13 (2606.07856) are all 2026 preprints; I did not look them up. They are plausible for the Nov 2026 date, but they are not older, widely cited works and several are single-purpose to the argument: [15] is described as 'the study closest to ours', [4] supplies the central RLVR evidence, and [13] and [8] are cited via paraphrase or a quoted phrase ('ampliﬁes but does not compound'). The CLAUDE.md protocol for this

title: Section 4.3 B-minus-A at seed 1 (+0.0) contradicts Table 2 (-0.7)
explanation:
Section 4.3 gives B minus A at round 4 as +0.0 pass@1 at seed 1. Table 2 reports the round-0 to round-4 change of pass@1 as -3.3 for A,1 and -4.0 for B,1. Round 0 is the same untrained model on the same exam partition, so B minus A should be -4.0 - (-3.3) = -0.7 (1 problem of 150), as it is at seed 0 (-3.3 - (-2.7) = -0.7, matching the quoted -0.7). Either the round-0 pass@1 of A and B differ at seed 1 (first-sample draws or patched scoring), in which case the comparison is not of changes and Table 2 does not show it, or one of the numbers is wrong. The interval [-2.7, +2.7] is centred on 0.0, so it is not a rounding artifact. Since this sentence is the only quantitative support for the 'patch has no effect' reading, the discrepancy should be resolved or explained (state the round-0 values for A and B).

Also (Sec 4.3 B-minus-A at seed 1 (+0.0) disagrees with Table 2 (-0.7)): Table 2 (10^-5, pass@1) gives A,1 = -3.3 and B,1 = -4.0, so B minus A at seed 1 is -0.7 (one problem), not +0.0. The seed-0 value is consistent (-3.3 minus -2.7 = -0.6, i.e. -0.67 = one problem). The interval [-2.7, +2.7] is centred on 0.0, so the text's seed-1 figure is internally coherent but not the table's. The Table 2 caption admits six values off by one problem, but this one is not listed and both numbers are used to argue 'no consistent effect'. Reconcile (and make the sign statement 'pas

title: Defect-rate figures (15.5-18.4%, 'a fifth', 440->542, 94-98%) do not reconcile with Table 4 and pool sizes
quote: this defect rejects 15.5–18.4% of the
explanation:
In Table 4 the self-training 'all' rows have R0 = 18.3, 18.1, 18.3 and last-round = 15.7, 15.5, 16.8 (gold arms: 18.2/18.0 at R0, 21.5/20.2 last). The lower end 15.5 is a last-round value (A, seed 2), and 18.4 appears nowhere in Table 4 (R0 max is 18.3). The range therefore mixes round-0 and last-round values and one number not shown. The Summary/abstract 'about one in six' (16.7%) is fine, but the quoted range should be either 18.0-18.3 at round 0 or 15.5-18.3 across all rounds, with the source stated.

Also ('About a fifth' pool enlargement (440 -> 542) implies 18.8% / +23%, outside the quoted 15.): 542/440 = +23.2% enlargement; the share of V'-accepted examples that V rejects is 102/542 = 18.8%, above both the stated maximum 18.4% and Table 4's R0 values (18.0-18.3, computed over all 500 problems rather than the 350 selection problems). The difference is probably the selection-set vs all-500 basis, but the text never says so, and the same '(440 -> 542)' is repeated in Sec 5.3(iii) as 'about a fifth of the pool'. State the basis or give '+23%'.

Also (Inconsistent/underspecified pool-size figures for the defect effect): The paper says the defect 'rejects 15.5-18.4% of the generations V' accepts' and that it would enlarge the round-0 kept pool 'from 440 to 542'. 102 of 542 is 18.8%, outside the stated range, and 542/440 is +23%, which is closer to a quarter than 'about a fifth'. Section 4.1 also gives the isolated MATH-500 round-0 pool as 872 examples, so it is unclear to which run (k=8 vs k=4, which seed) 440/542 belongs. The numbers that anchor the abstract's 'about one in six' should be tied to specific runs 

Also ('94-98%' rejection on affected problems vs Table 4 affected-parseable values (87.2-95.1%)): Table 4's 'affected, parseable' rows for the three self-training runs show rt of 92.8 -> 87.2, 95.1 -> 93.5 and 92.3 -> 92.0, so 87-95%, partly below 94%. This is probably reconciled by the 29-34 unparsable-gold problems being at about 100% (which pulls the 54-62 total up), but that is never stated, and '94-98% in every round' is not checkable from Table 4. State the weighting or give the two subsets separately.

Also (Patch pool difference '3-4 examples (under 0.5%)' vs '0-4' elsewhere, and base unclear): Sec 3.2, 5.3(iii) and Limitations say 0-4 examples (against a round-0 pool stated as 440 in Sec 3.2/Table 3), and 3-4 of 440 is 0.7-0.9%, not under 0.5%. The 0.5% is true only for the 10^-5, k=8 pool (872, Sec 4.1; 3-4/872 = 0.34-0.46%), which is never named here. Sec 4.4 then says 0-3 at 5x10^-4. Name the pool each fraction refers to.

title: Reproducibility gaps: unsaved logs, unspecified V' and selection rules; 'only removes a training example' framing
quote: Token counts at generation
explanation:
Design P training logs, token counts at generation time and the per-sample outputs of the 1,536-token re-scorings were not saved, so the cap-hit and truncation statistics on which the 'finished vs capped' decomposition and the 12-30%/52-72% attributions rely cannot be regenerated. The V' rule for predictions without a box, the construction of the format probe, the generation engine and seeds, the exact selection rule (all accepted samples or deduplicated per problem; the pool contains up to k solutions per problem, which up-weights easy problems), and how exam problems with unparsable golds enter denominators are not specified. The number of selected examples per problem matters since 'all kept solutions are used', so training is dominated by easy problems repeated up to k times, a form of selection bias not discussed.

Also (Claim that false rejects 'only remove a training example' is at odds with the paper's own ): The Introduction justifies the SFT setting by saying a false reject only removes an example, implying lower stakes than RLVR. But a systematic false reject removes whole answer forms and whole problems from the pool (the paper's own 54-62 problems with 94-98% rejection), so SFT learns from a pool skewed toward parseable gold forms; this is the same directional bias the paper claims to study. The 'cheapest and most widely used form of the loop' is also asserted without citation. The contrast with

title: Optimizer-step count (~195) disagrees with pool sizes in Table 3
quote: so the round-2 model is a single adapter (about 195 optimizer
explanation:
The text says the round-2 model is one adapter trained on the round-1 pool, with about 195 steps for Run A at 5e-4. Table 3 caption states optimizer steps are half the pool, and the round-1 pools are 326 (seed 1) and 350 (seed 2), i.e. 163 and 175 steps. 195 would correspond to a pool of about 390, which matches neither seed (the round-0 pool, 440 and 424, gives 220 and 212 steps for the round-1 adapter). Possibly an average of the two adapters is intended, but then 'single adapter' is misleading. Dose is the central confound in the no-filter and train-on-gold comparisons (3-4x steps), so the step counts should be stated precisely.

Also (Optimizer-step count (~195) inconsistent with pool sizes and 'steps = half the pool'): Sec 3.4 and the Table 3 caption say optimizer steps are half the pool size. The round-2 model is trained on the round-1 pool, which Table 3 gives as 326 (seed 1) and 350 (seed 2) for Run A at 5x10^-4, i.e. about 163 and 175 steps. 195 steps would need a pool of ~390; the round-0 pool (440) would give 220. None of the stated numbers yields 195. Either the pool sizes in Table 3 or the step count is wrong (or the step count includes something not described).

title: Cap-hit range, Table 2 caption cross-reference and bootstrap resample counts are inconsistent
quote: The untrained model already hits the cap in 41–48% of MATH-500 generations,
explanation:
Table 1 caption gives round-0 cap-hit as 43.0-43.2% (seeds 1-2) and 48.2% (seed 3). The lower bound 41% does not appear in Table 1; it may come from the 10^-5 runs, which are not tabulated for cap-hit. Cite the source or use 43-48%.

Also (Table 2 caption points to Sec 3.4 for material not found there): Section 3.4 contains no discussion of recomputation differences, the six one-problem discrepancies, or a 'separate re-scoring' behind the matched column (the matched measure is introduced in Sec 4.5). The example given (B, seed 1 pass@8 58.0% vs 58.7%) also cannot be traced to any text number, and the six affected values are not identified, so the reader cannot tell whether headline numbers such as Sec 4.3's B-minus-A (x2-01) are among them.

Also (Table 2 caption cites Section 3.4 for off-by-one values and re-scoring that Section 3.4 do): The caption says six round values differ by one problem from recomputation and points to Section 3.4 for these and for the 'separate re-scoring' behind the matched column, but Section 3.4 contains neither (only a remark that 1,536-token re-scorings were not saved). It is also unclear which version enters the table: B,1 shows -1.3 for pass@k, which equals 58.0 - 59.3 on 150 problems only if one of 58.0/58.7 is used (58.7 minus the round-0 value would give about -0.6 or -0.7). A reader cannot tell

Also (Bootstrap resample count: Sec 3.4 says 10,000 for every within-run change, Table 4 uses 2,): Table 4 (the within-run changes in r_t) and the Table 2 matched column are stated to use 2,000 resamples, contradicting the blanket 'for every within-run change ... 10,000 resamples' in Sec 3.4. Not consequential for the numbers but the blanket statement is inaccurate.
